222.stem: Hot tea is poured into a cup. The temperature of tea can be modelled by $T=25+70(1.5)^{-0.4t}$, where $T$ is the temperature of the tea, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after it is poured.

parts.latex: What is the temperature of the tea 4 minutes after it has been poured?
At what rate is the tea cooling 4 minutes after it has been poured?
How long after the tea is poured will it take for its temperature to reach $55^\circ\text{C}$?

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} T &= 25 + 70(1.5)^{-0.4\times 4} \\ &= 61.5891\ldots \\ &\approx 61.6^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dT}{dt} = 70(1.5)^{-0.4t}(-0.4)\ln(1.5)$$
When $t = 4$,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= 70(1.5)^{-1.6}(-0.4)\ln(1.5) \\ &= -5.934\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Therefore at $t = 4$ the tea is cooling at $5.9^\circ\text{C}$ per minute.
criteria: Finds the derivative of $T$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} 55 &= 25 + 70(1.5)^{-0.4t} \\ \dfrac{30}{70} &= 1.5^{-0.4t} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right) &= -0.4t\ln(1.5) \\ t &= -\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{3}{7}\right)}{0.4\ln(1.5)} \\ &\approx 5.22 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ it takes approximately $5.22$ minutes.
criteria: Uses the log function to solve the equation
Makes $1.5^{-0.4t}$ the subject of the equation, or equivalent merit

232.stem:
The population of mice on an isolated island can be modelled by the function

$$m(t)=a\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{26}t\right)+b,$$

where $t$ is the time in weeks and $0\le t\le 52$. The population of mice reaches a maximum of 35 000 when $t=13$ and a minimum of 5000 when $t=39$. The graph of $m(t)$ is shown.

\exfigure{34_q31_1}

figures.cap: graph of m(t) for 0<=t<=52, max 35000, min 5000

parts.latex: What are the values of $a$ and $b$?

On the same island, the population of cats can be modelled by the function

$$c(t)=-80\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{26}(t-10)\right)+120.$$

Consider the graph of $m(t)$ and the graph of $c(t)$.

Find the values of $t$, $0\le t\le 52$, for which both populations are increasing.
Find the rate of change of the mice population when the cat population reaches a maximum.

criteria: Provides the correct value of $a$ or the correct value of $b$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides the correct values for $a$ and $b$

criteria: Finds the values of $t$ when the population of mice increases and the values of $t$ when the population of cats increases
Finds the values of $t$ when the population of mice increases, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The cat population reaches a maximum at $t = 36$.
$$m'(t) = \dfrac{\pi}{26}\times 15\,000\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{26}t\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} m'(36) &= \dfrac{\pi}{26}\times 15\,000\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{26}\times 36\right) \\ &= -642.7\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Therefore the mice population is decreasing at 643 mice per week.

160.stem:
The depth of water in a bay rises and falls with the tide. On a particular day the depth of the water, $d$ metres, can be modelled by the equation

$$d=1.3-0.6\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right),$$

where $t$ is the time in hours since low tide.

parts.latex: Find the depth of water at low tide and at high tide.
What is the time interval, in hours, between two successive low tides?
For how long between successive low tides will the depth of water be at least 1 metre?

solutions.latex:
$$d = 1.3 - 0.6\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Maximum depth (high tide)} &= 1.3 + 0.6 \\ &= 1.9 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Minimum depth (low tide)} &= 1.3 - 0.6 \\ &= 0.7 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the depth of water at either high or low tide, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \text{Period} &= \dfrac{2\pi}{\left(\frac{4\pi}{25}\right)} \text{ hours} \\ &= 12.5 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

$$d = 1.3 - 0.6\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)$$
When $d = 1$,
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 1.3 - 0.6\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right) \\ -0.3 &= -0.6\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right) \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= \cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right) \\ \dfrac{4\pi}{25}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \\ t &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \times \dfrac{25}{4\pi},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \times \dfrac{25}{4\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{25}{12},\ \dfrac{125}{12} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{267_q23_1}
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Time interval} &= \dfrac{125}{12} - \dfrac{25}{12} \\ &= 8\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one value of $t$ for $d = 1$, or equivalent merit
Attempts to solve the given equation when $d = 1$

195.stem:
A camera films the motion of a swing in a park.

Let $x(t)$ be the horizontal distance, in metres, from the camera to the seat of the swing at $t$ seconds.

The seat is released from rest at a horizontal distance of 11.2 m from the camera.

\exfigure{296_q26_1}

figures.cap: swing frame with seat released, camera at 11.2 m horizontal distance

parts.latex:
The rate of change of $x$ can be modelled by the equation
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-1.5\pi\sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}t\right).$$
Find an expression for $x(t)$.

Displacement, velocity and acceleration.reason: Integrating velocity dx/dt of the swing seat to get position x(t)

Rates of change using integration.reason: not_when: integrating a velocity belongs to Displacement, velocity and acceleration

parts.latex: How many times does the swing reach the closest point to the camera during the first 10 seconds?

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{dx(t)}{dt}=-1.5\pi\sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}t\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned}x(t)&=\int-1.5\pi\sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}t\right)dt\\&=\dfrac{-1.5\pi}{\frac{5\pi}{4}}\times\left(-\cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}t\right)\right)+k\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $x=11.2$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{So}\quad11.2&=1.2\cos(0)+k\\11.2&=1.2+k\\k&=10\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x(t)=1.2\cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}t\right)+10$$
criteria: Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Period}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{5\pi}{4}}\\&=1.6\end{aligned}$$
$$10\div1.6=6.25$$
$\therefore$ Number of complete periods in 10 seconds is 6.

$\therefore$ Reaches closest point to camera 6 times.
criteria: Finds the period, or equivalent merit

260.stem:
The moon is illuminated by reflected sunlight. The proportion of the moon which is illuminated each night can be approximately modelled by the function below:
$$M(t)=0.5\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}(t-13)\right)+0.5,$$
where $t$ is the time in days after midnight on the 1st of August.

parts.latex: Find the proportion of the moon which is illuminated at midnight on the following days:
14th August (that is, $t=13$)
29th August (that is, $t=28$)
Show that the time period between consecutive full moons is 30 days, according to the model provided here.
For $0\le t\le 30$, find the values of $t$ when the moon is not illuminated at all.
Sketch the graph of $M(t)$ for $0\le t\le 30$, showing any stationary points, points of inflection and intercepts with the axes.

solutions.latex:
When $t = 13$,
$$\begin{aligned} M(13) &= 0.5\sin 0 + 0.5 \\ &= 0.5 \end{aligned}$$

When $t = 28$,
$$\begin{aligned} M(28) &= 0.5\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}\times 15\right) + 0.5 \\ &= 0.5\sin\pi + 0.5 \\ &= 0.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} T &= \dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{15}} \\ &= 30 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$

When $M(t) = 0$,
$$\begin{aligned} 0.5\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}(t-13)\right) + 0.5 &= 0 \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}(t-13)\right) &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
For $0 \le t \le 30$,
$$-\dfrac{13\pi}{15} \le \dfrac{\pi}{15}(t-13) \le \dfrac{17\pi}{15}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{15}(t-13) &= -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t - 13 &= -7.5 \\ t &= 5.5 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{408_q28_s1}

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct sketch (ticks shown at the maximum $(20.5, 1)$ and the intercept $0.297$)

408_q28_s1.notes: Solution sketch drawn by Claude: M(t) for 0 <= t <= 30, minimum t = 5.5, inflections (13, 0.5) and (28, 0.5), maximum (20.5, 1), end points 0.297, dashed M = 0.5.

293.stem:
A rocket is returning back to Earth after completing a space mission.

Its distance from Earth can be modelled by the equation

$$S=55000\times 3^{-0.182t},$$

where $S$ is the distance from Earth in kilometres at time $t$ hours after it begins its return journey.

parts.latex: Find the speed of the rocket after 2 hours on its return journey.

When the rocket reaches a distance of 1000 km from Earth, a parachute is released.

How long, in hours, after the rocket begins its return journey does it release its parachute? Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} S'(t)=\dfrac{dS}{dt} &= -0.182\times\ln 3\times 55000\times 3^{-0.182t} \\ &= -10010\ln 3\times 3^{-0.182t} \end{aligned}$$

Speed of the rocket at time $t=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} S'(2) &= -10010\ln 3\times 3^{-0.182\times 2} \\ &= -7372.3576\ldots \\ \text{speed} &= |S'(2)| \approx 7372 \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ The speed of the rocket 2 hours after it begins its return journey is $7372 \text{ km/h}$.
criteria: Correctly differentiates to find an equation for speed, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: an absolute value was set equal to a negative number.

solutions.latex:
Let $S=1000$ and solve the equation for $t$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000 &= 55000\times 3^{-0.182t} \\ \dfrac{1}{55} &= 3^{-0.182t} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{55}\right) &= -0.182t\times\ln 3 \\ t &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{55}\right)\div(-0.182\times\ln 3) \\ &= 20.0419\ldots \\ &\approx 20.04 \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ The rocket deploys its parachute 20.04 hours after it begins its return journey.
criteria: Attempts to solve for $t$, or equivalent merit

88.stem: The decibel level of a sound is given by the formula: $$L=10\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}\right)$$ Where $L$ is the sound level in decibels, $I$ is the intensity of the sound in watts per square meter.

parts.latex:
A chocolate making machine produces a sound with intensity of $2.5\times10^{-5}\ W/m^2$.

Calculate the sound level of the machine to 4 decimal places.

A nearby industrial coffee grinder produced a sound that is 20 decibels louder than the chocolate making machine. What is the percentage increase in sound intensity produced by the coffee grinder compared to the chocolate making machine? Leave your answer to the nearest whole number.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} L &= 10\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{2.5\times10^{-5}}{10^{-12}}\right) \\ &= 73.9794 \text{ dB} \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Well done!

solutions.latex:
Coffee $=93.9794$ (i.e. 20 dB louder than the chocolate machine).

Find $I$:
$$\begin{aligned} 93.9794\ldots &= 10\log_{10}\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}} \\ \dfrac{93.9794\ldots}{10} &= \log_{10}\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}} \\ 10^{9.39794\ldots} &= \dfrac{I}{10^{-12}} \\ I &= 2.5\times10^{-3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \%\text{ increase} &= \dfrac{2.5\times10^{-3}-2.5\times10^{-5}}{2.5\times10^{-5}}\times100\% \\ &= 9900\% \end{aligned}$$

103.stem: The hours of daylight in Sydney can be modelled by: $$y(t)=2.24\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+1.34\right)+12.19,$$ where $y$, the number of hours of daylight and $t$, is the months of the year. (i.e.: $t=1$ represents January $1^{\text{st}}$; ignoring leap years)

$\therefore$ The longest day is in December.

544.stem:
A large rechargeable battery has a maximum storage capacity of 40 kWh when new.

After 1 year, the maximum storage capacity is 32 kWh.

The process of decay can be modelled by the function

$$y=ka^t$$

where $y$ is the maximum storage capacity of the battery, in kWh, $t$ years after it starts being used.

parts.latex: What are the values of $k$ and $a$?
Interpret the value of $a$ in this context.

solutions.latex:
Each year the maximum storage capacity is multiplied by $a=0.8$.

So each year the maximum storage capacity is $80\%$ of what it was the year before: it decreases by $20\%$ per year.

meta.concern: Either '80% retained each year' or '20% lost each year' should be accepted.

figures.cap: graph of y = k cos(ax+b) from 0 to 2pi

parts.latex:
Ben sketched the curve shown below to model a tidal experiment in his Science class.

Ben knows the curve is in the form $y=k\cos(ax+b)$ where $k>0$, $a>0$ and $0\le b\le\pi$.

By finding $k$, $a$ and $b$, write the equation for Ben’s tidal experiment.

\exfigure{1369_q23_1}

Transformations of trigonometric graphs.evidence: From the graph, 3 cycles take 2π, so the period is 2π/3
Transformations of trigonometric graphs.reason: Matching a transformed cos graph to its equation.

solutions.latex:
From the graph, 3 cycles take $2\pi$, so the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{a}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\\ a&=3\end{aligned}$$
The amplitude is $2$ and $k>0$, so $k=2$:
$$y=2\cos(3x+b)$$
The curve passes through $(0,-2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}-2&=2\cos b\\ \cos b&=-1\\ b&=\pi\quad(\text{since }0\le b\le\pi)\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=2\cos(3x+\pi)$$
criteria: Finds two of $k$, $a$, $b$, or equivalent merit
Finds one of $k$, $a$, $b$, or equivalent merit

639.stem: A saucepan of hot water at a temperature of $T^\circ$ Celsius loses heat when taken off the stove. It cools according to the equation $T=T_0+Ae^{kt}$ where $t$ is the time elapsed in minutes, $T_0$ is the room temperature measured in degrees Celsius and $k$ is a constant.

parts.latex: A saucepan of hot water of temperature $95^\circ$ is removed from the stove. It cools to a temperature of $90^\circ$ five minutes later in a room with a temperature of $27^\circ$. By finding the value of the constants $T_0$ and $A$, write an equation for $T$ in terms of $t$.
How hot will the water be after 10 minutes?

solutions.latex:
$T_0$ is the room temperature, so $T_0=27$.

Initially ($t=0$), $T=95$:
$$\begin{aligned}95&=27+Ae^{k(0)}\\A&=68\end{aligned}$$
When $t=5$, $T=90$:
$$\begin{aligned}90&=27+68e^{5k}\\63&=68e^{5k}\\e^{5k}&=\dfrac{63}{68}\\5k&=\ln\dfrac{63}{68}\\k&=\dfrac{1}{5}\ln\dfrac{63}{68}\\&=-0.01527459576\\&=-0.0153\ (3\text{ significant figures})\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T=27+68e^{-0.0153t}\quad(\text{or equivalent})$$
criteria: Correctly finds $A$ and $k$, or equivalent merit
Writes an exponential equation in the form $T=27+68e^{5k}$ or writes an equation to find $k$ in terms of $A$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the final equation had $e^{-0.153t}$; with $k=-0.0153$ it is $T=27+68e^{-0.0153t}$.

solutions.latex:
When $t=10$, with $k=\dfrac{1}{5}\ln\dfrac{63}{68}=-0.01527\ldots$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=27+68e^{10k}\\&=85.36764706\\&\approx 85^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The water will be about $85^\circ$ after 10 minutes.

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $T=27+68e^{-10k}$ should be $T=27+68e^{10k}$ (with $k<0$); the value $85.37$ is unchanged.

650.stem: The number of hours of daylight ($H$) in Sydney can be modelled by the trigonometric function $H=2.3\sin\big(0.005(\pi t-265)\big)+13.1$ where $t$ is the number of days after 1$^{\text{st}}$ January, 2025.

figures.cap: graph of H against t for 0 to 600

parts.latex: What is the maximum number of hours of daylight in Sydney in a year?
can_use: Maxima and minima from the range

parts.latex: How quickly are the number of hours of daylight increasing when $t=10$?

solutions.latex:
$H$ is greatest when the sine term equals 1:
$$\sin\big(0.005(\pi t-265)\big)=1$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \text{Maximum number of daylight hours}&=2.3\times 1+13.1\\&=15.4\end{aligned}$$

Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}H&=2.3\sin(0.005(\pi t-265))+13.1\\\dfrac{dH}{dt}&=0.0115\pi\cos(0.005(\pi t-265))\end{aligned}$$
When $t=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dH}{dt}&=0.0115\pi\cos(0.005(\pi\times 10-265))\\&=0.01416467195\\&\approx 0.0142\text{ hours/day}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the derivative of $H=2.3\sin\big(0.005(\pi t-265)\big)+13.1$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Find when $H=12$:
$$\begin{aligned}2.3\sin(0.005(\pi t-265))+13.1&=12\\2.3\sin(0.005(\pi t-265))&=-1.1\\\sin(0.005(\pi t-265))&=\dfrac{-1.1}{2.3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\text{reference angle}=0.4986733471$$

Billie is in another carriage. The height, $B(t)$, in metres above the ground of the top of her carriage is given by

$$B(t)=c-k\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\right),$$

where $c$ and $k$ are as found in part (a).

\exfigure{1628_q28_s1}

The centre line $c$ is midway between 39 and 3, and the amplitude $k$ is half the difference:

solutions.latex:
$$\text{Period}=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{24}}=48$$
It takes 48 seconds.

The carriages are at the same height when $A(t)=B(t)$:
$$c-k\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}t\right)=c-k\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\right)$$
$$\therefore\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}t\right)=\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\right)$$
Two angles have equal cosines when they are equal, opposite, or add to $2\pi$ (within one revolution).

Equal angles:
$$\dfrac{\pi}{24}t=\dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)$$
which is impossible.

Opposite angles:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{\pi}{24}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\\ -\dfrac{\pi}{24}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{24}t-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\\ \dfrac{\pi}{12}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{4}\\ t &= 3\end{aligned}$$
Angles adding to $2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{24}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{24}(t-6)\\ -\dfrac{2\pi}{24}t &= -2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\\ \dfrac{\pi t}{12} &= \dfrac{9\pi}{4}\\ t &= 27\end{aligned}$$
When $t=3$:
$$\text{height}=21-18\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{24}=4.37 \text{ m}$$
When $t=27$:
$$\text{height}=21-18\cos\dfrac{27\pi}{24}=37.63 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Makes correct use of the periodic nature of cosine function, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le t\le 12\\ 0&\le\dfrac{\pi t}{7}\le\dfrac{12\pi}{7} &&\left(\text{multiply by } \dfrac{\pi}{7}\right)\end{aligned}$$

An electric vehicle with an empty battery is being recharged. The capacity, $C\%$, of the battery while charging at time $t$ minutes may be modelled by the equation

solutions.latex:
Substituting $C=35$ and $t=50$:
$$\begin{aligned} 35&=100\left(1-2^{-50k}\right)\\ 0.35&=1-2^{-50k}\\ 2^{-50k}&=0.65\\ -50k\ln(2)&=\ln(0.65) &&(\text{take } \ln \text{ of both sides})\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln(0.65)}{-50\ln(2)}\\ &=0.0124297\ldots\\ \therefore\ k&=0.01243 \text{ (4 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$

Substituting $C=90$ and $k=0.01243$:
$$\begin{aligned} 90&=100\left(1-2^{-0.01243t}\right)\\ 0.1&=2^{-0.01243t}\\ -0.01243t\ln(2)&=\ln(0.1) &&(\text{take } \ln \text{ of both sides})\\ t&=\dfrac{\ln(0.1)}{-0.01243\ln(2)}\\ &=267.2508\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The battery will be on charge for 267.25 minutes (2 dec. pl.), or 4 hours 27 minutes.

solutions.latex:
Initially ($t=0$), $C=0$.

For $k>0$, $2^{-kt}\to0$ as $t\to\infty$, hence $C\to100$ as $t\to\infty$.

Describing the rate of change using the first and second derivatives:
$$\begin{aligned} C'&=100k\ln(2)\times2^{-kt}\\ C''&=-100k^2(\ln2)^2\times2^{-kt} \end{aligned}$$
Given $k>0$, for all $t>0$:
$$\begin{aligned} C'&>0 &&\text{capacity increasing}\\ C''&<0 &&\text{rate of increase decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the battery charge capacity increases from 0 at a decreasing rate over time, but can never (theoretically) reach $100\%$ charge.

1013.stem:
Brendan is sitting in a cabin of a Ferris wheel which is revolving. The height, $B(t)$, in metres above the ground of her cabin is given by

$$B(t)=c-k\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{28}\right),$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds after Brendan's cabin first reaches the bottom of its revolution and $c$ and $k$ are constants.

\exfigure{1371_q15_1}

The top of each carriage reaches a greatest height of 28 metres and a smallest height of 4 metres.

figures.cap: illustration of a Ferris wheel

parts.latex: Find the value of $c$ and $k$.
How many seconds does it take for one complete revolution of the Ferris wheel?

solutions.latex:
Rearranging:
$$B(t)=-k\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{28}\right)+c$$
so $c$ is the centre and $k$ is the amplitude.

The centre is midway between the greatest and smallest heights:
$$c=\dfrac{28+4}{2}=16$$
The amplitude is the distance from the centre to the greatest height:
$$k=28-16=12$$
$$\therefore c=16,\ k=12$$

meta.marker_note: $\dfrac{1}{2}$ mark deducted if $k=-12$; 1 mark deducted if the values of $k$ and $c$ are switched. Many students struggled with this question.

solutions.latex:
One complete revolution is one period. Using period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ with $n=\dfrac{\pi}{28}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Period}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{28}}\\&=2\pi\times\dfrac{28}{\pi}\\&=56\text{ seconds}\end{aligned}$$

$$P(t)=180+44\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{183}\right)$$

where $t$ is the number of days after 22 March 2023, for $0\le t\le366$.
What is the \textbf{maximum} and \textbf{minimum} prices of petrol during the year?
Sketch the function $P(t)=180+44\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{183}\right)$ for $0\le t\le366$.

$$-1\le\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{183}\right)\le 1$$

$$\begin{aligned}P&=180+44\\&=224\text{ cents/litre}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Ian is cooking a pizza. The temperature of the pizza oven is modelled by the equation

$$T=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2t}$$

where $T$ is the temperature of the oven in $^\circ C$ at time $t$ minutes since the oven was switched on.
What is the initial temperature of the oven?
Calculate the average rate at which the temperature changes per minute from $t=25$ to $t=75$, correct to two decimal places.

Ian can place the pizza in the oven when the instantaneous rate of change of temperature is less than or equal to $1^\circ C$ per minute.

After turning on the oven, how long must Ian wait before he can place the pizza in the oven, correct to the nearest minute?

solutions.latex:
The oven is switched on at $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=175-150\times(0.9)^0\\&=25^\circ\text{C}\end{aligned}$$

At $t=25$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2(25)}\\&=86.4265\end{aligned}$$
At $t=75$:
$$\begin{aligned}T&=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2(75)}\\&=144.1163\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The average rate of change is the change in $T$ divided by the change in $t$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Average rate}&=\dfrac{144.1163\ldots-86.4265}{75-25}\\&=1.15\ ^\circ\text{C/min (2 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

The instantaneous rate is $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$. Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}a^{kt}=k\ln a\cdot a^{kt}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dT}{dt}&=-150\times0.2\ln(0.9)(0.9)^{0.2t}\\&=-30\ln(0.9)(0.9)^{0.2t}\end{aligned}$$
Require $\dfrac{dT}{dt}<1$:
$$\begin{aligned}-30\ln(0.9)(0.9)^{0.2t}&<1\\(0.9)^{0.2t}&<\dfrac{1}{-30\ln(0.9)}\\\ln(0.9)^{0.2t}&<\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{-30\ln(0.9)}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Dividing by $\ln(0.9)<0$ reverses the inequality:
$$\begin{aligned}0.2t&>\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{-30\ln(0.9)}\right)}{\ln(0.9)}\\0.2t&>10.9227\\t&>54.6\\t&>55\text{ min (nearest min)}\end{aligned}$$
Ian must wait 55 minutes.

1231.stem:
The average monthly maximum temperature in Sydney can be modelled using the cosine function, $T=A\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)+B,$ where $T$ is the average maximum temperature and $t$ is the time elapsed since the start of the year in months (where $0\leq t\leq 12$).  The lowest average maximum temperature throughout the year is $17^\circ$ and the highest average maximum temperature is $27^\circ$ (in January).  The graph showing the average monthly maximum temperature is shown below.

\exfigure{566_q10_1}

figures.cap: graph of T against t for 0 to 12 months: maximum 27 at t = 0 and t = 12, minimum 17 at t = 6

parts.latex: Find the value of $A$ and the value of $B$.
State the period of the function.

An outdoor music festival is being planned.  The event is to be held when the average maximum temperature is at least $24^\circ$.  For what values of $t$ can the event take place?  Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is half the difference between the highest and lowest temperatures:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}(27-17)\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $T=27$ (January):
$$\begin{aligned}27&=5\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi(0)}{6}\right)+B\\B&=22\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct value of $A$ or $B$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ with $n=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Period}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}\\&=12\end{aligned}$$

The temperature is $24^\circ$ when
$$\begin{aligned}5\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)+22&=24\\5\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)&=2\\\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)&=\dfrac{2}{5}\end{aligned}$$
Cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants ($0\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\le 2\pi$).

First quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=1.159279481\\t&=2.214060718\end{aligned}$$
Fourth quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=2\pi-1.159279481\\&=5.123905826\\t&=9.785939282\end{aligned}$$
From the graph, the temperature is at least $24^\circ$ at the start and end of the year:
$$\therefore\ 0\le t\le 2.21\ \text{ or }\ 9.79\le t\le 12$$
criteria: Obtains one correct value of $t$, or equivalent merit

An astronomer is attempting to predict the height of a satellite above the ground as it orbits around the Earth. Using precise measurements, the height of the satellite can be modelled with the function:

1371.stem:
An electric vehicle with an empty battery is being recharged. The capacity, $C\%$, of the battery while charging at time $t$ minutes may be modelled by the equation:

$$C = 100(1 - 2^{-kt})$$

The battery is charged at $35\%$ capacity after 50 minutes.

parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is $0.01243$, correct to 4 significant figures.
To prolong the life of the battery, the charger may be set to switch off when the battery reaches $90\%$ capacity. For how long will the battery be on charge until it reaches $90\%$ capacity?
By considering the first and second derivative, describe the behaviour of $C$ for $t \ge 0$ if the battery is left on charge indefinitely.

Concavity and points of inflection.evidence: C''<0 ... increases from 0 at a decreasing rate
Concavity and points of inflection.reason: Sign of C'' interpreted as concavity.

Increasing and decreasing functions.evidence: C'>0 ... the battery charge capacity increases

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the guideline used $t$ for the unknown constant ($2^{-50t}$, $t=0.01243$); it is $k$.
meta.concern: source solution writes t in place of k throughout (2^{-50t}, t = 0.01243); rewritten with k

solutions.latex:
Initially $C=0$. Since $k>0$, $2^{-kt}\to 0$ as $t\to\infty$, so $C\to 100$ as $t\to\infty$.
$$\begin{aligned} C'&=100k\ln 2\times 2^{-kt}\\ C''&=-100k^2(\ln 2)^2\times 2^{-kt} \end{aligned}$$
Since $k>0$, $C'>0$ and $C''<0$ for all $t\ge 0$.

Hence, the battery charge capacity increases from 0 at a decreasing rate over time, but can never reach $100\%$ charge.

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dT}{dt}&=70\times(-0.4)e^{-0.4t}\\ &=-28e^{-0.4t}\end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-28e^{-0.4\times4}\approx-5.65\ ^{\circ}\text{C/min}$$

1385.stem: In Canberra, the average daily temperature $T$ in degree Celsius $(^{\circ}\text{C})$ in Canberra is represented by the formula $T=7\sin(nx+1.5)+13$, where $n$ is a constant value and $x$ is the number of the month of the year (i.e. January = 1, February = 2 ,….)

parts.latex: As per this model, what are the highest and lowest average monthly temperatures in Canberra?
Find the exact value of $n$, given that the function has a period of 12.
Which month experiences the lowest average monthly temperature?
Sketch the graph of the function $T=7\sin(nx+1.5)+13$ for $1\le x\le 12$.

$$-1\le\sin(nx+1.5)\le1$$
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \text{Lowest average temp.}&=7\times(-1)+13=6^{\circ}\text{C}\\ \text{Highest average temp.}&=7\times1+13=20^{\circ}\text{C}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the lowest or the highest temperature, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The period of $\sin(nx+1.5)$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{n}&=12\\ n&=\dfrac{2\pi}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\ &\approx0.52\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Accept exact value or $0.52$.

1519.stem: Trout are released into a lake for the first time. The size of the population, $P$, of the trout can be modelled by the function $P=\dfrac{A}{1+15e^{-0.5t}}$, where $t$ is the time in months after the trout are introduced into the lake.

parts.latex: Initially, 250 trout were released into the pond. Show that $A=4\,000$.
Find the range of the function $P$.
At what rate is the population growing two months after the trout were released into the Lake? Give your answer correct to the nearest number of trout.

How many months will it take for the population of trout to exceed $3\,000$?

Give your answer as a whole number.

solutions.latex:
Initially $t=0$ and $P=250$:

$$\begin{aligned} 250 &= \dfrac{A}{1+15e^{-0.5(0)}} \\ 250 &= \dfrac{A}{16} \\ A &= 4000 \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 mark (no marking criteria shown in source)

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.5t}\to 0$, so $P\to\dfrac{4000}{1+15(0)}=4000$.

Since $1+15e^{-0.5t}>1$, $P$ never reaches $4000$.

Since $t\ge 0$, the smallest value is $P=250$, at $t=0$.

$$\therefore\ 250\le P<4000$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 mark (no marking criteria shown in source)
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: range given as $250\le P\le 4000$; $P$ never reaches 4000, so $250\le P<4000$.

solutions.latex:
Rewrite $P=4000\left(1+15e^{-0.5t}\right)^{-1}$ and differentiate (chain rule):

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 4000(-1)\left(1+15e^{-0.5t}\right)^{-2}(-0.5)(15e^{-0.5t}) \\ &= \dfrac{30000e^{-0.5t}}{\left(1+15e^{-0.5t}\right)^2} \end{aligned}$$

When $t=2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= \dfrac{30000e^{-0.5(2)}}{\left(1+15e^{-0.5(2)}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{30000}{e\left(1+15e^{-1}\right)^2} \\ &= 259.7601\ldots \\ &\approx 260 \text{ trout per month} \end{aligned}$$

So the population is increasing at approximately $260$ trout per month.

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $259.76\ldots$ was given as 259 (truncated); to the nearest trout it is 260.

solutions.latex:
Find when $P=3000$:

$$\begin{aligned} 3000 &= \dfrac{4000}{1+15e^{-0.5t}} \\ 1+15e^{-0.5t} &= \dfrac{4}{3} \\ 15e^{-0.5t} &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ e^{-0.5t} &= \dfrac{1}{45} \\ -0.5t &= \ln\dfrac{1}{45} \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln 45}{0.5} \\ &= 7.613324\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$P$ is increasing, so it exceeds $3000$ after $7.61$ months, which is $8$ months as a whole number.
criteria: Correct equation solved for $t$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is the initial number of toxic cells in the bloodstream?
Determine the time it takes for the number of toxic cells in the bloodstream to first exceed 200 per litre. Give your answer to the nearest hour.

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$:
$$D(0)=12\times1.16^0=12$$
The initial number is 12 toxic cells per litre.

Require $D(t)>200$:
$$\begin{aligned}12\times1.16^t&>200\\1.16^t&>\dfrac{200}{12}\end{aligned}$$
Take logarithms of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned}t\log_{10}(1.16)&>\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{200}{12}\right)\\t&>\dfrac{\log_{10}\left(\frac{200}{12}\right)}{\log_{10}1.16}\\&=18.9557\ldots\end{aligned}$$

1604.stem:
Natalie and her friends have made a post-HSC adventure bucket list. One of their bucket list items is to visit the Figure Eight rock pools and a visit to Figure Eight rock pools requires extreme caution. At all times it is very important to check the depth of water before entering the pools.

The depth of water at Figure Eight rock pools can be modelled by the equation

$$d=2+\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\,,\ \text{for } 0\le t\le12$$

where $d$ is in metres and $t$ is time after 7 am.

parts.latex: What is the depth of the water at high tide?

Figure Eight rock pools is only safe to visit when the depth of the water is below 1.75 m.

Between what times is it safe to visit the pools?

solutions.latex:
High tide is when $d$ is greatest, that is when $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}d&=2+\dfrac{1}{2}(1)\\&=\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The depth of water at high tide is $2.5$ m.

The pools are safe when $d<1.75$:
$$\begin{aligned}2+\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&<1.75\\\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&<-0.25\\\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&<-0.5\end{aligned}$$
Solve $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t=-0.5$. The related angle is $\sin^{-1}(0.5)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and sine is negative in the 3rd and 4th quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6} &&\text{so } t=7\\\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{11\pi}{6} &&\text{so } t=11\end{aligned}$$
By checking the graph or testing values, $d<1.75$ for $7<t<11$.

As $t$ is the number of hours after 7 am, $t=7$ is 2 pm and $t=11$ is 6 pm.

$\therefore$ It is safe to visit the pools between 2 pm and 6 pm.
criteria: Solves for the values of $t$ using trigonometric equation techniques, or equivalent merit
Makes $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t$ the subject, or equivalent merit

The period of $\cos(nt)$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$; here $n=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:

solutions.latex:
The function is $h(t)=3\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+13$, so the amplitude is $3$ and the centre line is $h=13$.

The period is given by
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Period}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ &=12\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The depth is at most $11$ m when $h(t)\le 11$. First solve $h(t)=11$.
$$\begin{aligned}3\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+13&=11 \\ \cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}&=-\dfrac{2}{3}\end{aligned}$$
The reference angle is $\cos^{-1}\dfrac{2}{3}\approx 0.8411$, and cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants. For the first cycle, $0\le t\le 12$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi t}{6}&\approx \pi-0.8411,\ \pi+0.8411 \\ &\approx 2.3005,\ 3.9827 \\ t&\approx 4.394,\ 7.606 \\ &\approx 4\text{ h }24\text{ min},\ 7\text{ h }36\text{ min}\end{aligned}$$
Since $t$ is the number of hours after 4 am, add 4 hours:
$$\begin{aligned}4{:}24+4\text{ h}&=8{:}24\text{ am} \\ 7{:}36+4\text{ h}&=11{:}36\text{ am}\end{aligned}$$
Between these times $\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\le-\dfrac{2}{3}$, so $h\le 11$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the family can be at the beach from } 8{:}24\text{ am until } 11{:}36\text{ am}$$

1852.stem: The temperature, $T$ degrees, of a liquid is increasing according to the model $T(t)=20+Ae^{kt}$, where $t$ is time in hours. The initial temperature of the liquid is 35 degrees.

parts.latex: Show that $A=15$.
After 4 hours, the temperature of the liquid is 80 degrees. Show that $k=\ln\sqrt{2}$.
Find the rate at which the temperature is increasing after 4 hours.

Hence, sketch the graph $T(t)=20+15e^{\ln\sqrt{2}t}$.

\exfigure{464_q21_1}

solutions.latex:
The initial temperature is the value at $t=0$, so $T(0)=35$.
$$\begin{aligned}35&=20+Ae^{0} \\ 35&=20+A \\ A&=15\end{aligned}$$

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks

solutions.latex:
After $4$ hours $T(4)=80$, with $A=15$:
$$\begin{aligned}80&=20+15e^{4k} \\ 60&=15e^{4k} \\ 4&=e^{4k} \\ 4k&=\ln 4 \\ k&=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 4\end{aligned}$$
Using the log law $n\ln a=\ln a^n$, and $4=2^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}k&=\ln 4^{\frac{1}{4}} \\ &=\ln\left(2^2\right)^{\frac{1}{4}} \\ &=\ln 2^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\ln\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Solves for $k$ as $\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 4$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{kt}=ke^{kt}$ with $k=\ln\sqrt{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}T'(t)&=15\ln\sqrt{2}\,e^{\ln\sqrt{2}\,t} \\ T'(4)&=15\ln\sqrt{2}\,e^{4\ln\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{4\ln\sqrt{2}}=e^{\ln(\sqrt{2})^4}=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}T'(4)&=15\ln\sqrt{2}\times 4 \\ &=60\ln\sqrt{2} \\ &=30\ln 2 \\ &\approx 20.8\end{aligned}$$

1884.stem:
Anubhav is doing some research on the number of patients emergency waiting rooms across all NSW hospitals at any given time. He notices that the number of patients, $P$, can be modelled by the function $P(t)=a\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)+b$, where $t$ is the time since 12 am. The maximum number of patients is $2500$ and the minimum is $700$. The graph of $P(t)$ is shown below.

\exfigure{388_q27_1}

figures.cap: graph of P(t): cosine curve from 2500 at t=0 down to a minimum of 700 and back up to 2500 at t=c

parts.latex: What are the values of $a$ and $b$ in the equation and $c$ on the graph?
Between what times (to the nearest minute) each day are there less than $1000$ patients in emergency waiting rooms across all NSW hospitals?

solutions.latex:
The graph is a cosine curve starting at its maximum $2500$, with minimum $700$.
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{2500-700}{2}=900 &&(\text{amplitude}) \\ b&=\dfrac{2500+700}{2}=1600 &&(\text{centre line})\end{aligned}$$
$c$ is the end of one full period:
$$\begin{aligned}c&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ &=12\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=900,\ b=1600,\ c=12$$
criteria: Finds two of $a$, $b$ and $c$, or equivalent merit
Finds one of $a$, $b$ and $c$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Source rubric: 1 mark for each variable.
meta.source_flag: The question names the function $M(t)$ but the graph axis and the text call the quantity $P(t)$ (inconsistency in the paper; question not changed).

solutions.latex:
There are fewer than $1000$ patients when $900\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+1600<1000$. First solve for equality:
$$\begin{aligned}1000&=900\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+1600 \\ -600&=900\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6} \\ -\dfrac{2}{3}&=\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\end{aligned}$$
The reference angle is $\cos^{-1}\dfrac{2}{3}=0.841\ldots$, and cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants. For the first period, $0\le t\le 12$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi t}{6}&=\pi-0.841,\ \pi+0.841 \\ t&=\dfrac{6(\pi-0.841)}{\pi},\ \dfrac{6(\pi+0.841)}{\pi} \\ &=4.39\ldots,\ 7.60\ldots \\ &\approx 4{:}24,\ 7{:}36\end{aligned}$$
Between these times $\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}<-\dfrac{2}{3}$. The period is $12$ hours, so the same happens $12$ hours later.
$$\therefore\ \text{fewer than } 1000 \text{ patients between } 4{:}24\text{ am and } 7{:}36\text{ am, and between } 4{:}24\text{ pm and } 7{:}36\text{ pm}$$
criteria: Finds both values of $t$ in the first period, or equivalent merit

1923.stem:
A circular Ferris wheel rotates at a constant rate, and the height of a certain passenger above the ground as a function of time can be modelled by the equation:

$$h(t)=20\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{20}(t-15)\right)+22,$$

where $h(t)$ represents the height in metres and t is the time in seconds.

parts.latex: What is the maximum height of the person during the ride?
Show that the Ferris wheel completes 15 full rotations during a 10-minute ride.
A passenger can view the harbour from any height above 30m. After the Ferris wheel starts the ride, when will the passenger reach height of 30m for the first time?
How long will the passenger stay above 30m during the 10-minute ride? Answer in minutes and seconds.

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is $20$ and the centre line is $y=22$, so
$$h_{\max}=22+20=42 \text{ m}$$

For $h(t)=20\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{20}(t-15)\right)+22$ the period is
$$T=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{20}}=40 \text{ seconds}$$
A 10-minute ride lasts $10\times60=600$ seconds, so the number of rotations is
$$\dfrac{600}{40}=15$$
criteria: Finds the period $40$ seconds, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Solve $h(t)=30$ for the first $t\ge0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 20\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{20}(t-15)\right)+22 &= 30 \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{20}(t-15)\right) &= \dfrac{2}{5} \end{aligned}$$
Let $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{20}(t-15)$. At $t=0$, $\theta=-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, and $\theta$ increases with $t$. On $-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\le\theta\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ the first solution of $\sin\theta=0.4$ is $\theta=\sin^{-1}(0.4)\approx0.4115$ (the other solutions below this lie before the ride starts).
$$\begin{aligned} t-15 &= \dfrac{20}{\pi}\times0.4115 \\ t &\approx15+2.62 \\ &\approx17.6 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

meta.self_check: python: t=17.6198; h(0)=7.86 so no earlier crossing.

solutions.latex:
In each cycle the passenger is above $30$ m when $\sin\theta>0.4$, that is for
$$\sin^{-1}(0.4)<\theta<\pi-\sin^{-1}(0.4)$$
This is an angle of $\pi-2\sin^{-1}(0.4)\approx2.318$, and $\theta$ changes by $\dfrac{\pi}{20}$ per second, so the time above $30$ m in one cycle is
$$\dfrac{2.318}{\frac{\pi}{20}}\approx14.76 \text{ seconds}$$
There are $15$ full cycles in the ride (part (b)).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{time} &\approx15\times14.76 \\ &\approx221.4 \text{ seconds} \\ &\approx3 \text{ minutes } 41 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the time above $30$ m in one cycle, or equivalent merit

2005.stem:
The predicted number of cases, $C$ of Capona virus strain present in country X, $n$ days after it was first detected is predicted by the model:

$$C=5e^{3n}+1$$

parts.latex: How many cases were present when the virus strain was first detected?
Find the rate at which the number of cases is predicted to be increasing on the 10th day.
State when is the number of cases predicted to first exceed 2 000.

solutions.latex:
When the strain is first detected, $n=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}C&=5e^0+1\\ &=6\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 6\text{ cases}$$

The rate of increase is $\dfrac{dC}{dn}$ (cases per day):
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dC}{dn}&=5e^{3n}\cdot3\\ &=15e^{3n}\end{aligned}$$
The first day is $n=0$, so the $10$th day is $n=9$:
$$\dfrac{dC}{dn}=15e^{27}\text{ cases/day}$$

$$\begin{aligned}5e^{3n}+1&=2000\\ 5e^{3n}&=1999\\ e^{3n}&=\dfrac{1999}{5}\\ 3n&=\ln\dfrac{1999}{5}\\ n&\approx1.997\end{aligned}$$
The number of cases exceeds $2000$ when $n>1.997$, so this first happens at $n=2$, the $3$rd day.

Ms Iacona notices that the number of emails she receives per week from students is cyclical. Every 12 weeks she receives the highest number of emails.

The number of emails Ms Iacona receives each week, $f(t)$, is modelled by the function

$$f(t)=a\cos(bt)+c$$

where $t$ is the number of weeks after 1 January 2023 and $0\le t\le 52$.

The lowest number of emails Ms Iacona receives is 15 per week and the highest number of emails per week is 45.

The number of emails is at a maximum on 1st January 2023 i.e., when $t=0$.

Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is half the difference between the highest and lowest values.
$$a=\dfrac{45-15}{2}=15$$
The period is $12$ weeks.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{b}&=12\\b&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
So $f(t)=15\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)+c$. The maximum is at $t=0$, so $f(0)=45$.
$$\begin{aligned}45&=15+c\\c&=30\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=15,\ b=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ c=30$$
criteria: Finds two of $a$, $b$, $c$ correctly, or equivalent merit

The relative level of a noise compared to a reference level is calculated by the formula

$$R=20\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{N}{N_0}\right),$$

where $R$ is the relative noise level measured in decibels (dB), $N$ is the level of a noise and $N_0$ is the maximum noise level permitted.

The relative noise level at a construction site when operating machinery was found to be 8 dB higher than the maximum noise level permitted.

Show that the level of noise produced by the machinery was approximately 2.5 times greater than the maximum noise level permitted.

solutions.latex:
Put $R=8$ in the formula.
$$\begin{aligned} 8 &= 20\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{N}{N_0}\right) \\ \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{N}{N_0}\right) &= \dfrac{2}{5} \\ \dfrac{N}{N_0} &= 10^{0.4} \\ &\approx 2.51 \end{aligned}$$
So $N\approx2.51\times N_0$: the noise level is approximately 2.5 times the maximum permitted level.

2493.stem:
An iron has accidently been left on. Fortunately, it switches itself off automatically after a period of inactivity.

The temperature of the iron can be modelled by the equation $T = 20 + 155(1.2)^{-0.4t}$, where $T$ is the temperature of the iron's surface, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after the iron switches itself off.

parts.latex:
What is the temperature of the iron $8$ minutes after it has switched off ?

Give your answer to the nearest degree.

At what rate is the temperature of the iron's surface changing after $8$ minutes ?

(Give your answer to one decimal place.)
How long, to the nearest minute, will it take for the iron to cool to $36^\circ\text{C}$ ?
What will be the eventual temperature of the iron ?

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=8$.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 20 + 155(1.2)^{-0.4(8)} \\ &\approx 106^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}a^{kt} = k a^{kt}\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= -0.4\left(155(1.2)^{-0.4t}\right)\ln(1.2) \\ &= -62(1.2)^{-0.4t}\ln(1.2) \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 8$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= -62(1.2)^{-3.2}\ln(1.2) \\ &\approx -6.3^\circ\text{C/min} \end{aligned}$$

Set $T=36$ and solve for $t$, taking logarithms of both sides.
$$\begin{aligned}36 &= 20 + 155(1.2)^{-0.4t}\\ 16 &= 155(1.2)^{-0.4t}\\ \dfrac{16}{155} &= 1.2^{-0.4t}\\ \ln\left(\dfrac{16}{155}\right) &= -0.4t\ln(1.2)\\ t &= \dfrac{-\ln\left(\frac{16}{155}\right)}{0.4\ln 1.2} \\ &\approx 31\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t \approx 31 \text{ minutes}$$
criteria: Obtains $\dfrac{16}{155} = 1.2^{-0.4t}$ or an expression for $t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
High tide to low tide is half a period, so the period is $T=12$.

solutions.latex:
The curve has the form $y=k\cos(ax+b)$.

The amplitude is $2$ and $k>0$, so $k=2$.

The graph completes $3$ cycles for $0\le x\le 2\pi$, so $a=3$.

When $x=0$, $y=-2$:
$$\begin{aligned} -2&=2\cos b \\ \cos b&=-1 \\ b&=\pi \end{aligned}$$
This is the value with $0\le b\le\pi$.
$$\therefore\ y=2\cos(3x+\pi)$$
Equivalently, from the graph, there is a phase shift of $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the left, giving $y=2\cos 3\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$.

As a transformation of $y=\cos x$: dilate in the $y$ direction by a factor of $2$ (replace $y$ by $\dfrac{y}{2}$), dilate in the $x$ direction by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$ (replace $x$ by $3x$), and translate $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the left (replace $x$ by $x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}$):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{y}{2}&=\cos 3\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ y&=2\cos 3\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \end{aligned}$$

On any given day, the depth of water in a river is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right),\ 0\leq t\leq 24$$

The minimum of $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)$ is $-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} h_{\min} &= 14-8 \\ &= 6 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum depth is } 6 \text{ metres}$$

Set $h(t)=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} 14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) &= 10 \\ 8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) &= -4 \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, with $0\le \dfrac{\pi t}{12}\le 2\pi$.
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{12}=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ t=14 \text{ or } t=22$$

A weight is attached to a spring that is connected to the ground. The weight is pushed down towards the ground, and then released so that it bounces up and down.

3302.stem:
On a given day, the height of the water in a river is modelled by the function

$$h(t) = 5 + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right),$$

where $h$ is the height of the water, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 12 am.

solution sketch: sketch of h(t) over [0,24]

parts.latex: What is the height of the water at 12 am?

Sketch the graph of $h(t) = 5 + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$ in the domain $[0, 24]$.

A family decides to go on a picnic by the river from 12 pm to 2 pm. It is only safe to swim in the river if the height of the water is less than 4 metres.

When is the earliest time the family can swim in the river after 12 pm? Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
At 12 am, $t = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} h &= 5 + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\times 0\right) \\ &= 5 + 3\sin 0 \\ &= 5 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h = 5 \text{ m}$$

For $h = 5 + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$, the period is
$$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{n} = \dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{4}} = 8$$
The amplitude is 3, so the maximum value is $5+3 = 8$ and the minimum value is $5-3 = 2$.

\exfigure{1612_q24_s1}
criteria: Any two of: the period; the maximum and minimum values; the correct graph shape, or equivalent merit
Any one of the above points

solutions.latex:
Set $h = 4$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= 5 + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}t\right) \\ -\dfrac{1}{3} &= \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}t\right) \end{aligned}$$
The reference angle is $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \approx 0.3398$. Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, so
$$\dfrac{\pi}{4}t = \pi + 0.3398,\ 2\pi - 0.3398,\ 3\pi + 0.3398,\ 4\pi - 0.3398,\ \ldots$$
$$t = \dfrac{4}{\pi}(\pi + 0.3398),\ \dfrac{4}{\pi}(2\pi - 0.3398),\ \dfrac{4}{\pi}(3\pi + 0.3398),\ \dfrac{4}{\pi}(4\pi - 0.3398),\ \ldots$$
$$t \approx 4.433,\ 7.567,\ 12.43,\ 15.57,\ \ldots \text{ hours}$$
The family is at the river from 12 pm to 2 pm, that is $12 \le t \le 14$, so $t = 12.43$ is the first time it is safe to swim.

Since $12.43$ hours is 12 hours and 26 minutes, the earliest time is 12:26 pm.
$$\therefore\ \text{12:26 pm}$$

3360.stem:
An office has climate control and the temperature at any time $t$ hours is $T$ degrees Celsius, where

$$T(t)=22+3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)\qquad t\in[0,24]$$

parts.latex: What are the minimum and maximum temperatures in this office?

parts.latex:
Miss Kim brought her lunch into the office but forgot to place it in the refrigerator. The food will be spoilt if the surrounding room temperature is greater than $23.5^\circ$C for more than 3 hours.

Let $t=0$ correspond to the time which Miss Kim arrives at the office (8:00 am). What is the latest time that she should finish eating the lunch, before the food is spoilt?

solutions.latex:
Since $-1\le\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)\le1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Minimum}&=22-3=19^\circ\text{C}\\\text{Maximum}&=22+3=25^\circ\text{C}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the minimum or the maximum, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{12}}=24$ hours.

Find when $T=23.5$:
$$\begin{aligned}23.5&=22+3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)\\\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{\pi}{12}t=\dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ or } \pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
so $t=2$ or $t=10$.

The temperature is above $23.5^\circ$C from $t=2$, that is from 10 am.

$\therefore$ the latest time she should finish eating is 1 pm.

parts.latex:
The Richter scale defines the magnitude of an earthquake as $M=\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I}{S}\right)$ where $I$ is the intensity of the earthquake wave, and $S$ is the intensity of the smallest detectable wave.

An earthquake that registered 6.4 in magnitude was followed by another which was 4 times more intense.

Determine the magnitude of the second earthquake accurate to 1 decimal place.

solutions.latex:
For the first earthquake:

$$6.4=\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I_1}{S}\right)\text{, so } \dfrac{I_1}{S}=10^{6.4}$$

The second earthquake has $I_2=4I_1$.

$$\begin{aligned} M_2&=\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I_2}{S}\right)\\ &=\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{4I_1}{S}\right)\\ &=\log_{10}\left(4\times10^{6.4}\right)\\ &=\log_{10}4+6.4\\ &\approx 7.0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the magnitude is } 7.0 \text{ (to 1 decimal place).}$$

3694.stem:
The Richter scale is used to measure the magnitude of earthquakes. The magnitude $R$ of an earthquake is proportional to the logarithm of the ground displacement $d$ caused by the earthquake in millimetres. This relationship can be described by the equation:

$$R=\log_{10}(1000d)$$

parts.latex: In July 2022, an earthquake in the Easter Island region caused a ground displacement of 6310 mm. What was its magnitude on the Richter scale? Give your answer correct to one decimal place.
How many times larger is the ground displacement of an earthquake with a magnitude of $3.2$ compared to an earthquake with a magnitude of $1.6$? Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $d=6310$ into the given formula.
$$\begin{aligned} R&=\log_{10}(1000\times6310)\\ &=6.80002\ldots\\ &\approx6.8\end{aligned}$$

Rewrite $R=\log_{10}(1000d)$ in index form, $1000d=10^R$.

For magnitude $3.2$:
$$d_1=\dfrac{10^{3.2}}{1000}$$
For magnitude $1.6$:
$$d_2=\dfrac{10^{1.6}}{1000}$$
The ratio is
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d_1}{d_2}&=\dfrac{10^{3.2}}{10^{1.6}}\\ &=10^{1.6}\\ &\approx40\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about 40 times larger}$$
criteria: Writes expressions for $d_1$ and $d_2$, or equivalent merit

3700.stem:
The human heart pumps blood through the body by repeatedly contracting, which pushes blood out of the heart, and then relaxing, which lets new blood flow into the heart. The average human heart contains 50 mL of blood when contracted and 120 mL when relaxed. The total volume $V$ mL of blood in the heart at time $t$ seconds can be modelled by the function

$$V=35\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{3}t\right)+c$$

where $c$ is a constant. The diagram below shows the graph of $V(t)$ for $0\le t\le 4$.

\exfigure{1343_q32_1}

figures.cap: graph of V(t) for 0 to 4

parts.latex: Write down the value of $c$.
Calculate the period of $V$.
Calculate the rate of change of volume when $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$. Give your answer correct to the nearest millilitre per second.
What is the total volume of blood which is pumped out of the heart between $t=\dfrac{2}{7}$ and $t=\dfrac{3}{7}$? Give your answer correct to the nearest millilitre.
By considering the volume of blood in the heart between $t=0$ and $t=\dfrac{3}{7}$, or otherwise, determine what fraction of the time the heart contains at least $102.5$ mL of blood.

solutions.latex:
The volume oscillates between $50$ and $120$, so $c$ is the midpoint.
$$c=\dfrac{50+120}{2}=85$$

meta.format_note: Reason line for c added (midpoint of 50 and 120); consistent with source value.

solutions.latex:
The period is $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ with $n=\dfrac{7\pi}{3}$.
$$T=2\pi\div\dfrac{7\pi}{3}=\dfrac{6}{7}$$
The period is $\dfrac{6}{7}$ s.

Differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-35\times\dfrac{7\pi}{3}\sin\left(\dfrac{7\pi t}{3}\right)$$
When $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt}&=-\dfrac{245\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{6} \\ &=-\dfrac{245\pi}{3}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{245\pi}{6} \\ &\approx 128 \text{ mL/s} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct derivative and substitution of $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
At $t=\dfrac{2}{7}$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=35\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{2}{7}\right)+85 \\ &=35\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}+85 \\ &=67.5 \end{aligned}$$
At $t=\dfrac{3}{7}$, which is half a period, the volume is at its minimum, $V=50$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Volume pumped out}&=67.5-50 \\ &=17.5 \\ &\approx 18 \text{ mL} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the volume at $t=\dfrac{2}{7}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Set $V=102.5$.
$$\begin{aligned} 35\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi t}{3}\right)&=17.5 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi t}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The first time this occurs is when $\dfrac{7\pi t}{3}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so $t=\dfrac{1}{7}$.

Over $0\le t\le\dfrac{3}{7}$ (half a period), the volume is at least $102.5$ for $0\le t\le\dfrac{1}{7}$.
$$\text{Fraction of time}=\dfrac{\frac{1}{7}}{\frac{3}{7}}=\dfrac{1}{3}$$

3736.stem: Rumour spreading at a school can be modelled by $N=2\times 1.61^{0.7t}$ where $N$ is the number of students who have heard the rumour and $t$ is the number of hours after it first started.

parts.latex: How many students would have heard the rumour 6 hours after it started?
How long would it take all 165 Year 12 students to hear the rumour?

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=6$ into the model.
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 2\times 1.61^{0.7\times 6} \\ &= 14.78\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 14 \text{ or } 15 \text{ students (both accepted)}$$

meta.marker_note: Both 14 and 15 students accepted.
meta.format_note: Source criterion 'Both 14 and 15 students accepted' moved to marker_note.

solutions.latex:
Set $N=165$ and solve for $t$.
$$\begin{aligned} 165 &= 2\times 1.61^{0.7t} \\ \dfrac{165}{2} &= 1.61^{0.7t} \end{aligned}$$
Take natural logarithms of both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln\left(\dfrac{165}{2}\right) &= \ln\left(1.61^{0.7t}\right) \\ &= 0.7t\ln 1.61 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{165}{2}\right)}{0.7\ln 1.61} \\ &= 13.23\ldots \\ &\approx 13.24 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 13.24 \text{ hours}$$
criteria: Takes logarithms to obtain $\ln\left(\dfrac{165}{2}\right)=0.7t\ln 1.61$, or equivalent merit

3752.stem:
Fish are introduced into a small dam. The size of the population, $N$, of fish can be modelled can be modelled by the function

$$N=\dfrac{500}{1+24e^{-0.5t}}$$

where $t$ is the time in months after the fish are introduced into the dam.

parts.latex:
Show that the rate of growth of the size of the population is given by

$$\dfrac{dN}{dt}=\dfrac{6000e^{-0.5t}}{(1+24e^{-0.5t})^2}$$
Find the range of the function $N$, justifying your answer.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=500 & v&=1+24e^{-0.5t}\\ u'&=0 & v'&=-12e^{-0.5t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dN}{dt}&=\dfrac{(1+24e^{-0.5t})\cdot 0-500\times(-12e^{-0.5t})}{(1+24e^{-0.5t})^2}\\ &=\dfrac{6000e^{-0.5t}}{(1+24e^{-0.5t})^2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Quotient rule working with one error, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: No marks are awarded for the final line, but the statement must be written.

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$:
$$N=\dfrac{500}{1+24}=20$$
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.5t}\to 0$, so
$$N\to\dfrac{500}{1+24\times 0}=500$$
Since $\dfrac{dN}{dt}>0$ for all $t$, $N$ is always increasing, so it rises from 20 towards 500 without reaching it.
$$\therefore\ 20\le N<500$$
criteria: Finds the limiting value $N=500$, or equivalent merit

On any given day, the depth of water in a lake is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right),\ 0\le t\le 24$$

where $h$ is the depth of water, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 6 am.

figures.cap: blank axes for sketch of h(t)
solution sketch: worked sketch of h(t)

parts.latex: Find the values of $t$ for which $h(t)=10$.
What rate is the depth of the river changing at 1:00 pm?

solutions.latex:
Setting $h(t)=10$:
$$\begin{aligned} 14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)&=10\\ 8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)&=-4\\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $0\le t\le 24$, $0\le\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\le 2\pi$. Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants:
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{12}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ t=14 \text{ or } t=22$$
criteria: Finds one correct value of $t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiating using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} h'(t)&=8\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$t$ is measured from 6 am, so 1:00 pm is $t=7$.
$$h'(7)=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{12}\right)\text{ m/h}$$
$$\therefore\ h'(7)\approx -0.54 \text{ m/h}$$

4094.stem:
The population of salmon in a salmon farm grows and reduces as fish are born and sold.

The population $P$ is given by $P = 500\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) + 900$ where $t$ is time in days.

parts.latex: Determine the initial population.
What is the minimum number of salmon in the farm at any time?
How many days will it take for salmon population to first reach 1150?

solutions.latex:
The initial population is at $t = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 500\cos(0) + 900 \\ &= 1400 \end{aligned}$$

The minimum occurs when $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) = -1$.
$$\begin{aligned} P_{\min} &= -500 + 900 \\ &= 400 \end{aligned}$$

Set $P = 1150$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1150 &= 500\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) + 900 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For the first time, take the smallest positive angle.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi t}{4} &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ t &= \dfrac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 1\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ days}$$

4132.stem: The population of an island is increasing according to the formula $P=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}$ where $P$ is the population in thousands and $t$ is the time in years after January 1st 2020.

parts.latex: Find the initial rate of change of the population of the island.
Use the model to predict the population on 1st January 2040, correct to the nearest thousand.
Using the model, predict in what year will the population reach 40 000.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating the population formula:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}\\\dfrac{dP}{dt}&=10\times\dfrac{1}{50}e^{\frac{t}{50}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{5}e^{\frac{t}{50}}\end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$:
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{5}e^0=\dfrac{1}{5}$$
$P$ is in thousands, so initially the population is increasing at a rate of $200$ people per year.

On 1 January 2040, $t=20$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=20+10e^{\frac{20}{50}}\\&\approx 34.9182\end{aligned}$$
The predicted population on 1 January 2040 is $35\,000$.

The population is $40$ thousand, so $P=40$.
$$\begin{aligned}40&=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}\\e^{\frac{t}{50}}&=2\\\dfrac{t}{50}&=\ln 2\\t&=50\ln 2\\&\approx 34.657\end{aligned}$$
The population will reach $40\,000$ during 2054.
criteria: Substitutes and starts solving the equation, or equivalent merit

4133.stem:
The height of water $h$ metres in a harbour can be modelled using the function below:

$h=4-A\sin(bt)$, where $t$ is the time in hours after midnight.

\exfigure{1306_q22_1}

At 2 am the height of water in the harbour is at its minimum.

At 6 am the height of water in the harbour is at its maximum.

figures.cap: graph of h against t, minimum 2 at t=2, maximum 6 at t=6, period 8

parts.latex: Find the values of $A$ and $b$.

A boat can only enter the harbour when the height of the water is more than 5 metres.

Express the information given as an equation, and solve the equation to find the first time the boat can enter the harbour.

solutions.latex:
The minimum is at 2 am and the maximum at 6 am, so the minimum height is $2$ and the maximum is $6$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{amplitude}&=\dfrac{6-2}{2}\\&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore A=2$$
Half a period is $4$ hours (from minimum to maximum), so the period is $8$ hours.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{b}&=8\\b&=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore A=2,\ b=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$
criteria: At least one correct value, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The boat can enter when $h>5$, so first solve $h=5$ with $A=2$, $b=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned}5&=4-2\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\\\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{4}&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi t}{4}&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\&=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\\t&=\dfrac{28}{6},\ \dfrac{44}{6}\end{aligned}$$
The first time is $t=\dfrac{28}{6}=4\text{ h }40\text{ min}$.
$$\therefore\text{ the boat can first enter at } 4{:}40 \text{ am}$$
criteria: Sets up the equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A weight is attached to a spring that is connected to the ceiling. The weight is pulled away from the ceiling and then released so that it bounces up and down.

Let the distance of the weight from the ceiling be $x$ metres. The spring stretches and contracts such that $x$ varies sinusoidally with time, between 1.2 metres and 1.8 metres. It takes 1 second for the weight to go from its highest point to its lowest point.

The motion of the weight can be modelled using a sine wave of the form:

$$x=a\sin(bt+c)+d$$

How far from the ceiling is the weight 2.7 seconds after it is at a high point?

solutions.latex:
Since $x$ is the distance from the ceiling, the high point is at $x=1.2$ and the low point is at $x=1.8$.

Amplitude and centre of motion:
$$a=\dfrac{1.8-1.2}{2}=0.3,\qquad d=\dfrac{1.8+1.2}{2}=1.5$$
The time from high to low is 1 s, which is half a period:
$$\text{period}=2\times 1=\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$$
so $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$.

Assuming the weight starts ($t=0$) at the centre of motion, the distance from the ceiling is modelled by
$$x=0.3\sin(\pi t)+1.5$$
The weight is at a high point when $x=1.2$, that is when $\sin(\pi t)=-1$, which first occurs at $t=1.5$.

The required time is 2.7 s after this:
$$1.5+2.7=4.2$$
When $t=4.2$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 0.3\sin(\pi\times 4.2)+1.5 \\ &\approx 1.676 \text{ m (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
As the period is 2, the same answer follows from $t=1.5+0.7$, that is $t=0.2$.
criteria: Substitutes the correct time to find $x$, with one error, or equivalent merit
Finds $t=1.5$ for the highest point (or equivalent), or equivalent merit
Finds $b=\pi$ and recognises that the highest point corresponds to $x=1.2$, or equivalent merit
Finds the amplitude and centre of motion, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Accept $t=4.2$, $2.2$ or $0.2$, or the equivalent for the $t$ used for the highest point.

$$h(t) = A\cos(bt) + d$$

parts.latex: Find the values of $A$, $b$ and $d$.
Between what times on Tuesday can the ship sail?

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$ (8am) the tide is low, $h=10$. At $t=6$ (2pm) it is high, $h=16$.

Amplitude and vertical shift:
$$\begin{aligned} |A| &= \dfrac{16-10}{2}=3 \\ d &= \dfrac{16+10}{2}=13 \end{aligned}$$
The graph starts at its minimum when $t=0$, so the cosine is reflected: $A=-3$.

Half a period is $6$ hours (low tide to high tide), so the period is $12$ hours:
$$b=\dfrac{2\pi}{12}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$$
Check: $h(0)=-3+13=10$ and $h(6)=3+13=16$.
$$\therefore\ A=-3,\ b=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ d=13$$

solutions.latex:
With $t$ in hours after 8am, $h(t)=-3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)+13$. The ship can sail when $h\ge 11.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} -3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)+13 &\ge 11.5 \\ -3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right) &\ge -1.5 &&(\text{subtract } 13) \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right) &\le \dfrac{1}{2} &&(\text{divide by } -3, \text{ reverse the inequality}) \end{aligned}$$
For the first cycle, $0\le t\le 12$ gives $0\le\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\le 2\pi$, and $\cos\theta\le\dfrac{1}{2}$ when $\dfrac{\pi}{3}\le\theta\le\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{3}\le \dfrac{\pi t}{6} &\le\dfrac{5\pi}{3} \\ 2\le t &\le 10 \end{aligned}$$
So the ship can sail from $2$ hours to $10$ hours after 8am.
$$\therefore\ \text{the ship can sail between 10am and 6pm.}$$

(Over the whole day the cycle repeats every 12 hours, so the channel is also deep enough from midnight to 6am and from 10pm to midnight; the answer above is the window inside the first cycle.)

A heated metal ball is dropped into a liquid. As the ball cools, its temperature, $T^\circ$C, $t$ minutes after it enters the liquid is given by,

$$T = 400e^{-0.05t} + 25,\ t \ge 0.$$

figures.cap: blank axes T against t

parts.latex: Find the initial temperature of the balls as it enters the liquid.
Find the value of $t$ for which $T = 200$, giving your answer to 3 decimal places.
Find the rate at which the temperature of the ball is decreasing after 50 minutes, giving your answer to 3 decimal places.
As it cools the ball will eventually approach what temperature?

Sketch the graph of $T$.

\exfigure{1311_q31_1}

solutions.latex:
The ball enters the liquid when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} T(0) &= 400e^{0}+25 \\ &= 425 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the initial temperature is } 425^\circ\text{C}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 400e^{-0.05t}+25 &= 200 \\ 400e^{-0.05t} &= 175 \\ e^{-0.05t} &= \dfrac{7}{16} \\ -0.05t &= \ln\left(\dfrac{7}{16}\right) &&(\text{take natural logs}) \\ t &= 20\ln\left(\dfrac{16}{7}\right) \\ &\approx 16.534 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 16.534\text{ minutes}$$

The rate of change of temperature is the derivative:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= 400\times(-0.05)e^{-0.05t} \\ &= -20e^{-0.05t} \end{aligned}$$
When $t=50$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= -20e^{-2.5} \\ &\approx -1.642 \end{aligned}$$
The negative sign means the temperature is falling.
$$\therefore\ \text{the temperature is decreasing at about } 1.642^\circ\text{C per minute.}$$

As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.05t}\to 0$, so $T\to 400(0)+25$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the ball approaches } 25^\circ\text{C}$$

The graph starts at $(0,425)$ from part (a), decreases at a decreasing rate (since $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-20e^{-0.05t}<0$ and its size shrinks), and approaches the horizontal asymptote $T=25$ from part (d).

4900.stem:
Between 8 am and 8 pm on July 18, 2021, the height of the tide in Sydney harbour was given by

$$h(t) = 1 + 0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) \text{ for } 0 \le t < 12$$

Where $h$ is the height of the tide in metres, and $t$ is in hours with $t = 0$ at 8 am

parts.latex: What is the period of $h(t)$
What was the height $h(t)$ at low tide, and at what time did this low tide occur
A cruise ship is only able to enter the harbour if the tide is at least 1.2 m. Find all the times between 8 am and 8 pm on July 18 2021 that the cruise ship was able to enter the harbour

solutions.latex:
For $h(t)=1+0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$, the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$ with $b=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Period} &= 2\pi\div\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= 2\pi\times\dfrac{6}{\pi} \\ &= 12 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The minimum value of $\sin$ is $-1$, so the minimum height is $1-0.4=0.6$ m.

The sine curve reaches its minimum at $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of the period:

$$\dfrac{3}{4}\times 12=9 \text{ hours}$$

So the time is $8 \text{ am}+9 \text{ hours}=5$ pm.

$$\therefore\ \text{low tide is } 0.6 \text{ m at } 5 \text{ pm}$$
criteria: Finds the minimum height or the time of low tide, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The ship can enter when $h\ge 1.2$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1+0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) &\ge 1.2 \\ 0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) &\ge 0.2 &&(\text{subtract } 1) \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) &\ge \dfrac{1}{2} &&(\text{divide by } 0.4) \end{aligned}$$

For $0\le t<12$, $0\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}t<2\pi$, and $\sin\theta\ge\dfrac{1}{2}$ when $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\theta\le\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}t &\le\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \\ 1\le t &\le 5 \end{aligned}$$

The times are $8+1=9$ am and $8+5=13$, that is, 1 pm.

$$\therefore\ \text{the ship can enter between 9 am and 1 pm}$$

Use your knowledge of trigonometric functions to answer the questions below.

The tide in Sydney on Monday May 13 can be modelled by a trigonometric curve in the form

$$h=A\sin[n(t+\varepsilon)]+C$$

where $t$ is in hours after midnight and $h$ is the height of the tide in metres. At 12am (midnight), the graph below starts with the tide measured at 1.29m. High tide of 1.69m occurs at 2.54am. Low tide of 0.46m occurs at 9:43am.

Determine the time when the tide is first at a height of 1.25 metres, after 12am. Write your answer to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
The centre of oscillation is midway between the high and low tides.
$$\begin{aligned} C&=\dfrac{1.69+0.46}{2} \\ &=1.075 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
(The average is the median for two values.)

The amplitude is the upper limit minus the centre.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=1.69-1.075 \\ &=0.615 \end{aligned}$$

The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$.

High tide to low tide is 2:54 am to 9:43 am, which is 6 h 49 min. This is half a period, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{period}&=2\times 6\text{ h }49\text{ min} \\ &=13\text{ h }38\text{ min} \\ &=13.63\text{ h}\ \left(=\dfrac{409}{30}\text{ h}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2\pi}{n}&=\dfrac{409}{30} \\ n&=\dfrac{30\times 2\pi}{409} \\ &=\dfrac{60\pi}{409} \\ &\approx 0.46 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the period from the high and low tide times, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
High tide is a maximum of $h=A\sin[n(t+\varepsilon)]+C$, which happens when $n(t+\varepsilon)=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

High tide is at 2:54 am, $t=2.9$, and $n=\dfrac{60\pi}{409}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{60\pi}{409}(2.9+\varepsilon)&=\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ 2.9+\varepsilon&=\dfrac{409}{120} \\ \varepsilon&=\dfrac{409}{120}-2.9=\dfrac{61}{120}\approx0.508 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds that the curve starts at the centre of oscillation 6 h 49 min before 2:54 am, or equivalent merit

5078.stem: A cup of coffee is cooling according to the following exponential formula $C=21+\left(74\times 3^{-0.2t}\right)$, where $C$ is the temperature in degrees Celsius and $t$ is the time in minutes since the coffee was poured.

Calculate the temperature of the coffee after 10 minutes, correct to the nearest degree.
After how many minutes, to the nearest minute, will the coffee first reach $50^\circ\text{C}$?

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}C&=21+\left(74\times 3^{-0.2\times 0}\right)\\ &=95^\circ\text{C}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}C&=21+\left(74\times 3^{-0.2\times 10}\right)\\ &=21+\left(74\times 3^{-2}\right)\\ &=29.2222\ldots\\ &\approx 29^\circ\text{C (to the nearest degree)}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}50&=21+\left(74\times 3^{-0.2t}\right)\\ \dfrac{29}{74}&=3^{-0.2t}\\ \log_3\left(\dfrac{29}{74}\right)&=-0.2t\\ t&=-5\log_3\left(\dfrac{29}{74}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=\dfrac{-5\ln\left(\frac{29}{74}\right)}{\ln 3}\\ &\approx 4\text{ minutes and 15 seconds}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 4\text{ minutes (nearest minute)}$$

parts.latex: At time ($t$ hours) after 12:00 am, the height ($h$ metres) of the deck of a boat above the level of the jetty is given by $h=2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)+1$. Find, correct to the nearest minute, the first time after 12:00 am when the deck of the boat is level with the jetty.

solutions.latex:
The deck is level with the jetty when $h=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)+1&=0 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants.
$$\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dots$$
So $t=\dfrac{25}{6},\ \dfrac{25}{3},\ \dots$

The first time is $t=\dfrac{25}{6}$ hours, which is 4:10 am.

meta.marker_note: Must have a stationary minimum point at $t=0$ and $t=40$.

solutions.latex:
The rate of change of height is the derivative of $h$.
$$\begin{aligned} R &= h'(t) \\ &= -35\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}\right)\left(-\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right)\right) \\ &= \dfrac{7\pi}{2}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right) \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating again gives the rate of change of $R$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dR}{dt} &= \dfrac{7\pi}{2}\times\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right) \\ &= \dfrac{7\pi^2}{20}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right) \end{aligned}$$
The maximum value of the cosine is $1$.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum of } \dfrac{dR}{dt} = \dfrac{7\pi^2}{20}$$
criteria: Correct expression for $R$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Set $h=50$.
$$\begin{aligned} 50 &= -35\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+35 \\ 15 &= -35\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right) \\ -\dfrac37 &= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right) \end{aligned}$$
The first time this happens is the first solution of the cosine equation.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi t}{10} &= \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac37\right) \\ t &= \dfrac{10}{\pi}\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac37\right) \\ &\approx 6.41\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 6 \text{ minutes } 25 \text{ seconds}$$

5940.stem:
The temperature, $T^\circ$ C, at a farm over the course of a day is modelled by

$$T(t)=22+8\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)$$

where $t$ if the time in hours after midnight, $0\le t\le 24$.

parts.latex: Find the temperature at midnight.
Find $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$, leave your answer in the simplest form.
Determine whether the temperature is initially decreasing or increasing.
Find the maximum temperature and determine the first time at which this occurs.
can_use: Maxima and minima from the range

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} T(0)&=22+8\cos\left(-\dfrac{4\pi}{12}\right) \\ &=22+8\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &=26^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

Using the chain rule on $T=22+8\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt}&=-\dfrac{8\pi}{12}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)\right) \\ &=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)\right) \end{aligned}$$

Initially means $t=0$. The sign of $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$ decides whether $T$ is increasing or decreasing.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt}&=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\left(-\dfrac{4\pi}{12}\right) \\ &=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{\pi\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ &>0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the temperature is initially increasing}$$
criteria: Correct derivative value at $t=0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The maximum of cosine is $1$, so
$$T_{\max}=22+8(1)=30^\circ\text{C}$$
This occurs when
$$\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)\right)=1$$
so $\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)=0$, giving $t=4$.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum temperature is } 30^\circ\text{C, first at } t=4 \text{ (4 am)}$$
criteria: Finds the maximum temperature, or equivalent merit
